authority_contract.student_depth: Teacher PPT material mapped in F0B and preserved at the level actually taught
authority_contract.chemistry_truth: Zumdahl, Zumdahl, and DeCoste, Chemistry 11e, within CED scope
authority_contract.source_gap_rule: Topic 1.4 retains the bounded F0D mixture-composition resolution; no unsupported analytical methods are added.

scope_guards.rule: Do not assess mass spectra containing multiple elements or peaks from species other than singly charged monatomic ions.
Do not require assignment of quantum numbers to electrons in subshells.
Do not require writing electron configurations for elements that are exceptions to the Aufbau principle.
Keep detailed ionic lattice structure and bulk-property treatment for CED Unit 2; Unit 1 focuses on valence patterns and typical ionic charges.

concepts.canonical_verified_statement: A mole is an amount of substance containing 6.022 × 10^23 specified entities.
concepts.source_reference: CED 1.1.A.2; Teacher PPT U1 pp. 50-62; Teacher PPT U2 pp. 26-37; Zumdahl 11e §§3.3-3.4
concepts.student_depth_note: Students should connect amount in moles to particle count and mass.

concepts.canonical_verified_statement: The Avogadro constant is 6.022 × 10^23 mol^-1 and connects moles to the number of constituent particles or formula units.
concepts.source_reference: CED 1.1.A.2; Teacher PPT U2 pp. 26-37; Zumdahl 11e §3.3
concepts.student_depth_note: Use entity type explicitly when converting between moles and particles.

concepts.canonical_verified_statement: Molar mass is the mass per mole of a substance, commonly expressed in grams per mole. For a substance, the numerical value of a particle or formula-unit mass in atomic mass units corresponds to its molar mass in grams per mole.
concepts.source_reference: CED 1.1.A.3; Teacher PPT U1 pp. 50-62; Zumdahl 11e §3.4
concepts.student_depth_note: Students calculate molar mass from atomic masses and formulas.

concepts.canonical_verified_statement: For a pure substance, amount in moles can be calculated from sample mass and molar mass using n = m/M, with the relationship rearranged as needed.
concepts.source_reference: CED 1.1.A.3; Teacher PPT U1 pp. 55-62; Zumdahl 11e §§3.3-3.4
concepts.student_depth_note: Retain dimensional-analysis reasoning and units.

concepts.canonical_verified_statement: Dimensional analysis uses conversion factors whose units cancel so that mass, moles, and particle count can be related consistently.
concepts.source_reference: CED 1.1.A; Teacher PPT U1 pp. 55-62; Zumdahl 11e §1.7 and Ch. 3 problem-solving sections
concepts.student_depth_note: Students should show unit cancellation rather than memorize isolated arithmetic recipes.

concepts.canonical_verified_statement: Isotopes are atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons and therefore different masses.
concepts.source_reference: CED 1.2.A; Teacher PPT U2 pp. 8-23; Zumdahl 11e §3.2
concepts.student_depth_note: Keep element identity tied to proton number.

concepts.canonical_verified_statement: For a sample containing a single element, a mass spectrum can reveal the masses of its naturally occurring isotopes and their relative abundances.
concepts.source_reference: CED 1.2.A.1; Teacher PPT U2 pp. 8-23; Zumdahl 11e §3.2
concepts.student_depth_note: Students identify isotope peaks and relative abundance from a single-element spectrum.

concepts.canonical_verified_statement: Relative isotopic abundance is the fraction or percentage of atoms of an element represented by a particular isotope in a naturally occurring sample.
concepts.source_reference: CED 1.2.A.1; Teacher PPT U2 pp. 8-23; Zumdahl 11e §3.2
concepts.student_depth_note: Abundance percentages used in a weighted average sum to 100%.

concepts.canonical_verified_statement: Average atomic mass is estimated as the sum of each isotopic mass multiplied by its fractional relative abundance.
concepts.source_reference: CED 1.2.A.2; Teacher PPT U2 pp. 8-23; Zumdahl 11e §3.2
concepts.student_depth_note: Students should reason about where the weighted average lies before calculating.

concepts.canonical_verified_statement: AP Chemistry Unit 1 does not require interpretation of spectra containing multiple elements or peaks from species other than singly charged monatomic ions.
concepts.source_reference: CED Topic 1.2 exclusion statement
concepts.student_depth_note: Do not build questions that require excluded multi-element or multiply charged-species interpretation.

concepts.canonical_verified_statement: A pure compound has a fixed elemental composition; its constituent atoms or ions occur in definite proportions represented by its formula.
concepts.source_reference: CED 1.3.A.1-1.3.A.2; Teacher PPT U2 pp. 42-66; Zumdahl 11e §§3.6-3.7
concepts.student_depth_note: Connect symbolic formulas to fixed particle-level ratios.

concepts.canonical_verified_statement: In any pure sample of a given compound, the mass ratio of its constituent elements is constant.
concepts.source_reference: CED 1.3.A.2; Teacher PPT U2 pp. 42-66; Zumdahl 11e §3.6
concepts.student_depth_note: Use the relationship to connect composition data to a pure compound.

concepts.canonical_verified_statement: The mass percent of an element in a pure compound is the mass contribution of that element divided by the total mass of the compound, multiplied by 100%.
concepts.source_reference: CED 1.3.A; Teacher PPT U2 pp. 42-51; Zumdahl 11e §3.6
concepts.student_depth_note: Students calculate both percent composition and element mass in a sample.

concepts.canonical_verified_statement: An empirical formula gives the lowest whole-number ratio of atoms of the elements in a compound.
concepts.source_reference: CED 1.3.A.3; Teacher PPT U2 pp. 52-66; Zumdahl 11e §3.7
concepts.student_depth_note: Distinguish empirical ratio from a molecular formula when both are discussed.

concepts.canonical_verified_statement: Elemental mass or percent-composition data can be converted to moles of each element and reduced to a simplest whole-number ratio to determine an empirical formula.
concepts.source_reference: CED 1.3.A; Teacher PPT U2 pp. 52-66; Zumdahl 11e §3.7
concepts.student_depth_note: Students must connect measured mass composition to particle ratios through moles.

concepts.canonical_verified_statement: A mixture contains two or more types of particles or substances in proportions that can vary from sample to sample.
concepts.source_reference: CED 1.4.A.1; Teacher PPT U2 pp. 42-51, 82; Zumdahl 11e §1.10
concepts.student_depth_note: Contrast variable mixture composition with fixed pure-substance composition.

concepts.canonical_verified_statement: Elemental composition data can be used to assess the purity or composition of a sample by comparing measured composition with the composition expected for a pure substance.
concepts.source_reference: CED 1.4.A.2; Teacher PPT U2 pp. 48-51; Zumdahl 11e §§3.6-3.7
concepts.student_depth_note: Keep treatment at the CED/PPT level; do not introduce unsupported analytical methods.

concepts.canonical_verified_statement: When components have different elemental mass fractions, the measured elemental composition of a mixture reflects the contributions of the components and can be used quantitatively to infer mixture composition.
concepts.source_reference: CED 1.4.A; Teacher PPT U2 pp. 42-51, 82 (partial); Zumdahl 11e §§1.10, 3.6-3.7
concepts.student_depth_note: This is the bounded F0D resolution for the partial PPT mapping.

concepts.canonical_verified_statement: An atom contains a positively charged nucleus made of protons and neutrons and negatively charged electrons outside the nucleus.
concepts.source_reference: CED 1.5.A.1; Teacher PPT U7 pp. 2-5; Zumdahl 11e §2.5
concepts.student_depth_note: Avoid treating the Bohr orbit picture as the modern literal electron model.

concepts.canonical_verified_statement: The magnitude of electrostatic attraction or repulsion increases with the magnitudes of the charges and decreases as the separation between charged particles increases; AP Chemistry uses Fcoulombic ∝ q1q2/r^2 as a qualitative and quantitative relationship.
concepts.source_reference: CED 1.5.A.2; Teacher PPT U7 pp. 63-64; Zumdahl 11e atomic-structure treatment
concepts.student_depth_note: Use charge and distance causally; do not conflate nuclear charge with effective nuclear charge.

concepts.canonical_verified_statement: An electron shell is a principal energy level associated with electron states at broadly similar energy and average distance from the nucleus.
concepts.source_reference: CED 1.5.A.3; Teacher PPT U7 pp. 2-19; Zumdahl 11e §§7.5, 7.9
concepts.student_depth_note: Shell language is a model for electron-energy organization, not a fixed circular orbit.

concepts.canonical_verified_statement: A subshell is a set of orbitals within a principal shell, designated s, p, d, or f, with characteristic relative energies and orbital capacities.
concepts.source_reference: CED 1.5.A.3; Teacher PPT U7 pp. 4-24; Zumdahl 11e §§7.5, 7.7, 7.9
concepts.student_depth_note: Use subshell occupancy to interpret electron configurations.

concepts.canonical_verified_statement: Core electrons occupy inner filled shells or subshells, whereas valence electrons occupy the outer electron levels most directly involved in bonding and chemical behavior.
concepts.source_reference: CED 1.5.A.3; Teacher PPT U7 pp. 12, 17-19; Zumdahl 11e §§7.9, 7.12
concepts.student_depth_note: Keep definitions connected to electron configuration and later periodic trends.

concepts.canonical_verified_statement: A ground-state electron configuration represents the arrangement of electrons in the lowest-energy available orbitals for an atom or ion.
concepts.source_reference: CED 1.5.A; Teacher PPT U7 pp. 6-36; Zumdahl 11e §§7.5, 7.9, 7.11
concepts.student_depth_note: Students should read and write configurations for atoms and ions within AP scope.

concepts.canonical_verified_statement: In constructing a ground-state electron configuration, electrons occupy lower-energy orbitals before higher-energy orbitals, subject to the rules governing orbital occupancy.
concepts.source_reference: CED 1.5.A.3; Teacher PPT U7 pp. 6-24; Zumdahl 11e §7.11
concepts.student_depth_note: Do not require configurations of elements that are Aufbau exceptions when the CED excludes them.

concepts.canonical_verified_statement: Ion electron configurations are obtained by accounting for electrons gained or lost; for cations, electrons are removed from the outermost occupied principal level before inner levels.
concepts.source_reference: CED 1.5.A; Teacher PPT U7 pp. 29-36; Zumdahl 11e §8.4
concepts.student_depth_note: Use charge bookkeeping and energy/distance reasoning.

concepts.canonical_verified_statement: The energy required to remove an electron depends on its attraction to the nucleus, including average electron–nucleus distance and shielding/effective nuclear charge.
concepts.source_reference: CED 1.5.A.4; Teacher PPT U7 pp. 47, 50-58, 63-64; Zumdahl 11e §7.12
concepts.student_depth_note: Use Coulombic reasoning qualitatively when comparing species.

concepts.canonical_verified_statement: Assigning quantum numbers to individual electrons in subshells is outside the assessed AP Chemistry scope for Topic 1.5.
concepts.source_reference: CED Topic 1.5 exclusion statement
concepts.student_depth_note: Do not create required retrieval or application tasks on quantum-number assignment.

concepts.canonical_verified_statement: Photoelectron spectroscopy measures electron binding energies by ejecting electrons with high-energy photons and analyzing the energy associated with electron removal.
concepts.source_reference: CED 1.6.A.1; Teacher PPT U7 pp. 71-80; Zumdahl 11e §7.12 supporting discussion
concepts.student_depth_note: Focus student work on interpreting atomic/ionic PES rather than instrument engineering.

concepts.canonical_verified_statement: The position of a PES peak corresponds to the binding energy or energy required to remove electrons from a particular subshell; more strongly bound electrons require more energy to remove.
concepts.source_reference: CED 1.6.A.1; Teacher PPT U7 pp. 71-80
concepts.student_depth_note: Axis direction must be read from the given spectrum rather than assumed from memory.

concepts.canonical_verified_statement: Within the AP model, the relative height or intensity of a PES peak is ideally proportional to the number of electrons in the corresponding subshell.
concepts.source_reference: CED 1.6.A.1; Teacher PPT U7 pp. 73-80
concepts.student_depth_note: Use relative electron counts to compare peak intensities.

concepts.canonical_verified_statement: A PES can be interpreted to infer occupied subshells and electron counts, allowing a spectrum to be connected to the ground-state electron configuration of an atom or ion.
concepts.source_reference: CED 1.6.A; Teacher PPT U7 pp. 73-80
concepts.student_depth_note: Students should move between spectrum and electron configuration.

concepts.canonical_verified_statement: For isoelectronic or otherwise comparable species, differences in nuclear charge and electron–nucleus attraction can shift electron binding energies and therefore PES peak positions.
concepts.source_reference: CED 1.6.A; Teacher PPT U7 pp. 77-80; Zumdahl 11e periodic-trend/Coulombic reasoning
concepts.student_depth_note: Use the species and axis provided; avoid a rote left/right rule detached from the graph.

concepts.canonical_verified_statement: When elements are arranged by atomic number, recurring electron-configuration patterns produce recurring chemical and physical properties across the periodic table.
concepts.source_reference: CED 1.7.A.1; Teacher PPT U7 pp. 44-45; Zumdahl 11e §§7.11-7.12
concepts.student_depth_note: Connect periodic position to ground-state electron structure.

concepts.canonical_verified_statement: Periodic trends can be explained by the combined effects of nuclear charge, shielding, electron–electron repulsion, and average distance of valence electrons from the nucleus.
concepts.source_reference: CED 1.7.A.2; Teacher PPT U7 pp. 46-64; Zumdahl 11e §7.12
concepts.student_depth_note: Use precise causal language and avoid treating 'effective nuclear charge' as simply identical to proton count.

concepts.canonical_verified_statement: Atomic radius generally decreases across a period as effective nuclear attraction on valence electrons increases and generally increases down a group as occupied principal shells place valence electrons farther from the nucleus.
concepts.source_reference: CED 1.7.A.2; Teacher PPT U7 pp. 46-49; Zumdahl 11e §7.12
concepts.student_depth_note: Students should explain trends using structure, not merely arrow memorization.

concepts.canonical_verified_statement: First ionization energy generally increases across a period and decreases down a group because electron removal becomes more difficult with stronger effective nuclear attraction and easier with greater distance and shielding.
concepts.source_reference: CED 1.7.A.2; Teacher PPT U7 pp. 50-58; Zumdahl 11e §7.12
concepts.student_depth_note: Account for local deviations using electron configuration and electron repulsion when relevant.

concepts.canonical_verified_statement: Successive ionization energies increase, and a large jump indicates that electron removal has moved from valence electrons to a more strongly bound inner shell or subshell.
concepts.source_reference: Teacher PPT U7 pp. 51-56; Unit 1 scoring-guide evidence; Zumdahl 11e §7.12
concepts.student_depth_note: Use as support for valence-electron count and likely ionic charge.

concepts.canonical_verified_statement: Electron affinity describes the energy change associated with adding an electron to a gaseous atom; periodic patterns can be interpreted with electron structure and electrostatic interactions.
concepts.source_reference: CED 1.7.A.2; Zumdahl 11e §7.12
concepts.student_depth_note: The teacher PPT emphasizes other trends more strongly, so keep treatment at CED depth.

concepts.canonical_verified_statement: Electronegativity is an atom's ability to attract shared electrons in a bond; it generally increases across a period and decreases down a group as nuclear attraction and electron distance change.
concepts.source_reference: CED 1.7.A.2; Teacher PPT U7 p. 59; Zumdahl 11e §§7.12, 8.2
concepts.student_depth_note: Use trend as a predictive model rather than an isolated arrow.

concepts.canonical_verified_statement: Cations are generally smaller than their parent atoms after electron loss, whereas anions are generally larger after electron gain; comparisons among isoelectronic species are explained primarily by differences in nuclear attraction.
concepts.source_reference: CED 1.7.A.2; Teacher PPT U7 pp. 65-70; Zumdahl 11e §8.4
concepts.student_depth_note: Distinguish ionic-radius reasoning from neutral atomic-radius trends.

concepts.canonical_verified_statement: Periodic patterns can be used to predict or estimate an element's properties when direct data are unavailable.
concepts.source_reference: CED 1.7.A.3; Teacher PPT U7 pp. 44-70; Zumdahl 11e §7.12
concepts.student_depth_note: Require explanation with an appropriate atomic-structure model when possible.

concepts.canonical_verified_statement: Writing electron configurations for elements that are exceptions to the Aufbau principle is outside the assessed AP Chemistry scope for Topic 1.7.
concepts.source_reference: CED Topic 1.7 exclusion statement
concepts.student_depth_note: Teacher examples beyond this boundary may be background only, not required assessment targets.

concepts.canonical_verified_statement: Patterns in chemical reactivity arise from interactions involving valence electrons and atomic nuclei; elements with analogous valence configurations often show related chemical behavior.
concepts.source_reference: CED 1.8.A.1-1.8.A.2; Teacher PPT U7 pp. 44-70; Zumdahl 11e §§7.12, 8.1
concepts.student_depth_note: Connect group patterns to electron structure rather than labels alone.

concepts.canonical_verified_statement: Elements in the same periodic-table group often form analogous compounds because they have related valence-electron configurations.
concepts.source_reference: CED 1.8.A.2; Unit 1 scoring-guide evidence; Zumdahl 11e periodicity/bonding sections
concepts.student_depth_note: Use representative main-group patterns without claiming every group member behaves identically in all chemistry.

concepts.canonical_label: Typical ionic charge from periodic position
concepts.canonical_verified_statement: For many main-group elements, typical monatomic ion charges can be predicted from valence-electron count and periodic-table position.
concepts.source_reference: CED 1.8.A.3; Teacher PPT U7 pp. 29-36, 44-70; Teacher PPT U1 pp. 20-41; Zumdahl 11e §8.4
concepts.student_depth_note: Use charge as a consequence of electron gain/loss and stable electron arrangements, without anthropomorphic 'wanting' language.

concepts.canonical_verified_statement: The formula of an ionic compound reflects a ratio of cations and anions whose total charge is electrically neutral.
concepts.source_reference: Teacher PPT U1 pp. 20-41; Teacher PPT U8 pp. 3-11; Zumdahl 11e §§2.6, 8.1
concepts.student_depth_note: Supports CED 1.8 charge-pattern reasoning and later ionic-compound structure work.

concepts.canonical_verified_statement: An ionic compound is held together by electrostatic attraction among oppositely charged ions; ion formation and charge pattern are distinct from the resulting lattice-scale attraction.
concepts.source_reference: Teacher PPT U8 pp. 3, 9-11; Zumdahl 11e §8.1
concepts.student_depth_note: Keep full lattice structure/properties for Unit 2; Unit 1 uses this only to connect ion charge to compound formation.
